name: Beta distribution
seoDesc: Beta distribution: work out mean from the parameter, α and the parameter, β. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the parameter, α and the parameter, β and the Beta distribution calculator solves for mean. It suits an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Beta distribution calculator work?
sections.html:
The Beta distribution calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mean in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the mode and the probability type); then you type in the parameter, α, the parameter, β and the sample length.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Beta distribution calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Mean=(parameter, α ÷ (parameter, α + parameter, β))
Variance=(parameter, α × parameter, β ÷ ((parameter, α + parameter, β ^ 2) × (parameter, α + parameter, β + 1)))
Median=(parameter, α, parameter, β)
Skewness=(parameter, α, parameter, β)
P(X ≤ x)=(X, parameter, α, parameter, β)
P(X < x)=(X, parameter, α, parameter, β)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Mode set to Probability calculator, Probability type set to P(X < x), Parameter, α = 10 and Parameter, β = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Mean = 0.5, Variance = 0.0119 and Standard deviation = 0.1091.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mean = 0.5, Variance = 0.0119 and Standard deviation = 0.1091 should be roughly the size you expected from Mode set to Probability calculator and Probability type set to P(X < x).

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Beta distribution calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the parameter, α and the parameter, β — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Beta distribution calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mean, derived from the parameter, α and the parameter, β. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Beta distribution calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the parameter, α and the parameter, β, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mean = 0.5. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Beta distribution calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
